B1.1.1.q: A warehouse worker wants a handheld scanner to talk to a tablet a couple of metres away, using very little battery. Which connection fits?
B1.1.1.why: Bluetooth is short-range (about 10 m) and low-power, for linking devices directly.

B1.1.2.q: A photographer needs to copy files from a camera to a laptop with a cable that also charges the camera. Which connection is this?
B1.1.2.why: USB is a wired standard that carries both data and power.

B1.1.3.q: A café wants customers to connect their own phones and laptops to the internet without any cables. Which connection should it provide?
B1.1.3.why: Wi-Fi connects many devices wirelessly to a router or access point.

B1.1.4.q: A video editing studio needs the fastest, most reliable link between its desktop PCs and file server, and nobody moves around. Which connection is best?
B1.1.4.why: Wired Ethernet (copper or fibre) is faster, more reliable and harder to intercept than wireless.

B1.2.q: A hospital's heart monitors must never drop their connection, while visitors just want to browse the web. What is the best match?
options: Ethernet for monitors, Wi-Fi for visitors
Bluetooth for monitors, Ethernet for visitors
B1.2.why: Connection choice depends on need: critical kit needs reliable wired links, and visitors need mobility.

B1.3.q: A school removes all network cables and goes Wi-Fi only to save money. What is a likely implication?
options: More security risk and possible slowdowns at busy times
No devices can move between rooms
B1.3.why: Choosing a connection affects security, cost and performance, not just convenience.

B1.4.q: Video editors complain that large file transfers over Wi-Fi are slow and sometimes fail. What change would most improve performance?
B1.4.why: Wired connections give higher speed, lower latency and more reliability than shared Wi-Fi.

B2.1.1.q: In an office network, each PC has its own cable to one central switch. One cable breaks. What happens?
options: Only that PC loses its connection
Data travels the other way round the loop
All PCs slow to a stop
B2.1.1.why: In a star topology each device has its own link, but if the central switch fails, everything stops.

B2.1.2.q: In a network, devices are connected in a closed loop and data passes around it in one direction. Which topology is this?
B2.1.2.why: A ring links devices in a loop, so one break can stop the whole ring.

B2.1.3.q: All devices share one backbone cable, and every device receives all the data sent. Traffic grows and collisions increase. Which topology is this?
B2.1.3.why: In a bus topology everything shares one cable, so heavy traffic causes collisions and one break stops the network.

B2.2.1.q: A runner's phone connects to their wireless earbuds and smartwatch by Bluetooth. What type of network is this?
B2.2.1.why: A Personal Area Network links one person's devices over a short range.

B2.2.2.q: A school's computers, printers and servers all sit on one site and use network hardware the school owns. What type of network is this?
B2.2.2.why: A LAN covers a single site using the organisation's own hardware.

B2.2.3.q: A bank links the networks in all its branches across the UK using lines leased from a telecoms company. What type of network is this?
B2.2.3.why: A WAN covers a large area and links LANs using third-party lines.

B2.2.4.q: A company with two offices wants to link them securely over the public internet rather than paying for leased lines. What should it use?
B2.2.4.why: A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel through the internet to a private network.

B2.3.1.q: Nurses need to move between wards with tablets and stay connected the whole time. Which network factor is the designer considering?
B2.3.1.why: User needs cover mobility, the applications users run and how many connect at once.

B2.3.2.q: A stock trading firm requires a network with under 5 ms latency and 99.99% uptime. Which factor is this?
B2.3.2.why: Specifications are the technical requirements the network must meet, such as speed, latency and uptime.

B2.3.3.q: A farm needs the network to reach sensors in fields far from the main building. Which factor is this?
B2.3.3.why: Connectivity is whether every device and site that needs to connect can do so reliably.

B2.3.4.q: A small charity weighs up the price of cabling, switches, ISP fees and paying someone to support the network. Which factor is this?
B2.3.4.why: Cost is the full cost of building and running the network.

B2.3.5.q: Backups that run during the working day slow everyone's connection. Scheduling them overnight makes better use of the bandwidth. Which factor is this?
B2.3.5.why: Efficiency is how well the network uses its bandwidth to avoid congestion and delays.

B2.3.6.q: A company checks that a new network will work with its existing printers, servers and software before buying it. Which factor is this?
B2.3.6.why: Compatibility is whether the network works with the hardware, software and protocols already in use.

B2.3.7.q: A school installs its new network over the summer holiday, testing it before staff return, so lessons aren't disrupted. Which factor is this?
B2.3.7.why: Implementation covers how long rollout takes, how it is tested and how much disruption it causes.

B2.3.8.q: After the network upgrade, staff no longer wait minutes for files to open and finish more work each day. Which factor improved?
B2.3.8.why: Productivity is how the network affects how much staff can get done.

B2.3.9.q: A law firm insists its network uses encrypted Wi-Fi, a firewall and separate guest access. Which factor is it prioritising?
B2.3.9.why: Security protects the network from unauthorised access, interception and attack.

B2.4.q: Wi-Fi in a busy open-plan office is slow because too many devices share one access point. What would most improve performance?
B2.4.why: Performance depends on hardware and set-up. More access points spread the load.

B3.1.1.q: A worker wants their email kept on the server and synced, so they can see the same inbox on their phone and laptop. Which protocol fits?
B3.1.1.why: IMAP keeps mail on the server and syncs it across devices. POP3 downloads it, and SMTP sends it.

B3.1.1.q: Which protocol is used to SEND an email from Outlook to the mail server?
B3.1.1.why: SMTP sends email; IMAP and POP3 retrieve it.

B3.1.2.q: A company drops its landline phones and makes all calls through Microsoft Teams over the internet. What technology is this?
B3.1.2.why: VoIP sends voice and video as data packets over the internet.

B3.1.3.q: Which protocol should an online banking site use so that logins can't be read if intercepted?
B3.1.3.why: HTTPS adds TLS encryption to HTTP.

B3.1.4.q: When you pay with Apple Pay, the shop receives a one-off token instead of your real card number. What is this an example of?
B3.1.4.why: Secure payment systems protect card data using encryption and tokenisation.

B3.2.q: Someone on an open café Wi-Fi network captures another customer's unencrypted login details. Which security issue is this?
B3.2.why: Unencrypted data in transit can be intercepted, altered or blocked.

B3.3.q: A gamer has very fast broadband for downloads but still sees a lag between pressing a button and the game reacting. What is the problem?
B3.3.why: Bandwidth is how much data per second; latency is the delay. High latency causes lag even on fast connections.

B3.4.1.q: A designer needs the company logo to have a transparent background on the website without losing sharpness. Which format suits it?
B3.4.1.why: PNG is lossless and supports transparency. JPEG suits photos.

B3.4.2.q: A recording studio needs uncompressed, full-quality audio for editing, even though the files are huge. Which format suits it?
B3.4.2.why: WAV keeps full quality; MP3 is compressed for streaming.

B3.4.3.q: A YouTuber uploads a file containing both video and audio streams compressed by codecs. Which format is it most likely in?
B3.4.3.why: MP4 is a container format holding video and audio streams.

B3.4.4.q: A user downloads a program to install on Windows. Which file type will it most likely be?
B3.4.4.why: Application file formats are OS-specific: .exe for Windows, .apk for Android, .dmg for macOS.

B3.5.1.q: A music streaming service shrinks songs by permanently removing sounds most people can't hear. Which compression is this?
B3.5.1.why: Lossy compression permanently removes some data for much smaller files.

B3.5.2.q: A company zips its spreadsheets before emailing them, and every number must come back exactly as it was. Which compression must it use?
B3.5.2.why: Lossless compression restores the original exactly, which is essential for documents and data.

B3.6.q: During a video call, software compresses the video before sending it and decompresses it for playback on the other side. What is this software?
B3.6.why: A codec (coder-decoder) compresses media for sending and decompresses it for playback.
